aBuc4AC7NmU.title: Ramadan Prep Series: The Fiqh of Fasting
aBuc4AC7NmU.one_line: A practical fiqh walk-through of Ramadan fasting: intention, nullifiers, disputed medical cases, concessions, expiations, sunnahs, tarawih and zakat al-fitr.
aBuc4AC7NmU.summary: He opens with a lament for the decline of Arabic, tying it to the fall of Syria as its stronghold and recounting his own rigorous training, and argues that the Quran and the Arabic language preserve each other. He then teaches the fiqh of fasting from slides. Ramadan fasting needs an intention from the night before, though waking for suhoor counts, and the Maliki view allows one intention for the month. He gives one rule for nullifiers: anything deliberately taken into the body that nourishes. He lists clear nullifiers and non-nullifiers, then his own views on disputed cases: inhalers, drops and non-nutritive IV lines do not break the fast, suppositories do. He explains the concessions (illness, travel, pregnancy and nursing, severe exhaustion), stresses that harming the body to fast is sinful, and sets out the major and minor expiations with dollar estimates. A long aside rebukes misuse of zakat, including masjids taking it. He closes with sunnahs of suhoor and iftar, fasting from sins, staying with the imam in tarawih, and flexible rulings on zakat al-fitr and the Eid prayer.

outline.heading: Arabic, nearly a thing of the past
outline.gist: No nafha in the year compares with Ramadan, and he wants a talk or two on it in Arabic to honour both the month and the language of the Quran, which has become almost a relic even in Arab lands. Scholars in Morocco, Mauritania, Kuwait and Egypt have recently raised the alarm.

outline.heading: Syria, the fallen stronghold
outline.gist: One cause is the fall of Arabic's stronghold, Syria, a country that loves the language and teaches every science in it. He studied all of medicine in Arabic and took years to learn the English terms.

outline.heading: Classical Arabic or a beating
outline.gist: As a boy his shaykh made them preach to trees, stones and animals. At school, in military uniform, answers had to be in classical Arabic; his teacher Omar al-Sabbagh spoke nothing else and punished any answer in dialect.

outline.heading: The Alfiyyah by page number
outline.gist: All his teachers mastered the arts of Arabic. He studied Ibn Malik's Alfiyyah with Ibn Aqil's commentary before university, and one of his scholars, who never attended school, knew the Alfiyyah and its commentaries by page number.

outline.heading: No ijazah without poetry
outline.gist: A hafiz holding an ijazah had to master Arabic, prosody and poetry: his shaykh would not sign his Quran ijazah until he composed classical verse. When the stronghold fell, that care declined, and the ummah must revive it.

outline.heading: Scripture only in translation
outline.gist: We revive Arabic not for itself but for the Quran, which cannot be understood without it. The Gospel was revealed to Isa in Hebrew, rendered into Greek, then Latin, then other languages, and no original remains.

outline.heading: A 1,400-year-old book you can still read
outline.gist: Try reading anything written in English, French or German in the sixth century; those languages have changed beyond recognition. With basic Arabic you can read and understand a 1,400-year-old book: the Quran preserved the language and the language preserved the Quran.

outline.heading: Intention: a voluntary fast can start late
outline.gist: He speaks of intention as fiqh, not as Ihsan. A voluntary fast needs no intention from the night: if you wake near noon having eaten nothing and decide to fast, it is accepted with the reward of the whole day.

outline.heading: Ramadan needs an intention from the night
outline.gist: For Ramadan the intention must be set the night before. For the Shafi'is that is every night, though it need not be spoken; waking for suhoor is itself the intention. Someone who forgot it was Ramadan and remembered after Fajr has no valid fast.

outline.heading: Malik: one intention for the month
outline.gist: To escape that strictness, Imam Malik allows one intention before Ramadan to cover the whole month. It is not complicated: if you know tomorrow is Ramadan and you will fast, you have intended, and forgetfully eating during the day is a gift from Allah.

outline.heading: One rule for what breaks the fast
outline.gist: Anything you deliberately take into your body that provides nourishment, in the medical sense, breaks the fast. Understand this rule and you are spared most questions.

outline.heading: The same questions every year
outline.gist: Every Ramadan people ask as if it were humanity's first: toothbrushing, eye drops, the same questions for fifteen years. Learn the fiqh of Ramadan once, settle on it, and share it, so the shaykhs do not come to dread the month.

outline.heading: Nullifier: deliberate eating and drinking
outline.gist: Eating or drinking on purpose, including deliberately swallowing water during wudu. Deliberateness is an intention only Allah sees; no one can judge your fast for you, it is between you and Him.

outline.heading: Nullifier: intercourse and ejaculation
outline.gist: Intercourse, or deliberately reaching climax, breaks the fast and requires an expiation as well as a make-up day. A wet dream during a daytime nap does not; just bathe and continue, and waking after the Fajr adhan without having bathed is no problem.

outline.heading: Nullifier: induced vomiting
outline.gist: Deliberately making yourself vomit breaks the fast; vomiting that simply happens does not. A sick person already has an excuse not to fast.

outline.heading: Nullifier: IV nutrition and blood
outline.gist: A saline drip or a blood transfusion breaks the fast. In illness that is excused, but doing it without cause would be a sin.

outline.heading: Nullifier: smoking
outline.gist: Any kind of smoking breaks the fast: cigarettes, shisha or a pipe.

outline.heading: Nullifier: menstruation and postnatal bleeding
outline.gist: If bleeding begins during the day, that day's fast is void and is made up later. These are the six well-known nullifiers.

outline.heading: Not a nullifier: toothbrushing
outline.gist: Brushing with paste, a miswak or an electric brush does not break the fast, unless you swallow the paste or water.

outline.heading: Not a nullifier: eating forgetfully
outline.gist: Whoever eats or drinks forgetfully was fed and given drink by Allah. Out of courtesy, let him finish his mouthful rather than remind him, though a fasting onlooker may be tempted by envy; once he remembers he must spit out what is in his mouth. Someone laying out a whole meal is another matter.

outline.heading: Not a nullifier: non-nutritive injections
outline.gist: A wet dream in sleep is natural. Intramuscular or subcutaneous injections that carry no nourishment, such as painkillers, antibiotics or vitamin B12, do not break the fast; insulin he discusses separately.

outline.heading: Not a nullifier: swallowing saliva
outline.gist: Swallowing saliva does not break the fast even if a lot gathers, though deliberately collecting it is disliked and unpleasant.

outline.heading: Not a nullifier: water left after wudu
outline.gist: Rinse your mouth in wudu as usual; the sunnah of exaggerated rinsing does not apply while fasting. Water that remains despite normal rinsing does no harm, but do not multiply wudu for its own sake.

outline.heading: Disputed: inhalers
outline.gist: He moves from agreed cases to disputed ones. Scholars differ, but he holds that an inhaler for asthma, COPD or another lung disease does not break the fast.

outline.heading: Disputed: eye and ear drops
outline.gist: Although some may reach inside, drops in the eye or ear, antibiotic or otherwise, do not break the fast in his view.

outline.heading: Disputed: non-nutritive IV lines
outline.gist: He changed his view last year: an IV antibiotic without saline does not break the fast in his view, though most scholars hold that anything entering a vein does. Someone receiving such treatment is usually too ill to fast anyway.

outline.heading: Dialysis patients should not fast
outline.gist: Someone on dialysis two or three times a week should not fast at all, given the harm and the fluids he needs during the day; he pays the expiation instead, and even after a transplant may never be able to fast. Preserving the body comes first here.

outline.heading: Suppositories, and erring on the safe side
outline.gist: Of the four disputed cases, he holds that inhalers and drops do not break the fast, while IV lines are case by case. Suppositories, he thinks, do break it, since anything entering either passage does, though some scholars disagree for antibiotic or haemorrhoid suppositories. Take the view you find sound; if ill, take the concession, and when in doubt count the day broken and make it up.

outline.heading: Concession: illness
outline.gist: Whoever is ill or travelling makes up the days later, and sometimes breaking the fast is obligatory because continuing would harm the sick person.

outline.heading: Harming the body is a sin
outline.gist: People hate breaking their fast in Ramadan, but if your doctor says fasting harms you, break it. Making yourself sicker to fast is wrong and sinful: the body is a trust, and you were not required to fast.

outline.heading: Concession: travel, stricter than prayer
outline.gist: Scholars are lenient on combining and shortening prayers even for short trips, but stricter about breaking the fast. To stay clear of the dispute, take the longest distance cited, about 82 kilometres.

outline.heading: Travel: how many days
outline.gist: The schools differ: three days for the Shafi'is and Hanbalis, perhaps a week for the Malikis, two weeks for Abu Hanifa. Ask before travelling, and avoid breaking unless needed, since many missed days are hard to make up; perhaps break only on the days of travel.

outline.heading: Concession: pregnancy and nursing
outline.gist: A pregnant or nursing woman may break her fast, but owes a fidyah for each day even if she makes it up within the year.

outline.heading: Concession: severe exhaustion
outline.gist: Ramadan is easier now that it falls in spring and winter, but in summer a labourer carrying loads up stairs in the heat should intend to fast each day and break only when exhaustion overwhelms him. Even if that happens every day of the month, there is no sin as long as he intended each morning.

outline.heading: Northern Europe's endless days
outline.gist: Brothers in Germany and Scandinavia during summer Ramadans had only three or four hours of night. He told them to intend the fast and break it when they could no longer work or study, then make it up. Other views, fasting by the nearest normal region or by Makkah, are not needed where we live.

outline.heading: You know yourself
outline.gist: Whether exhaustion has reached the point of harm or of failing your duties is between you and Allah, so there is no need to ask him: you know yourself. These are the four concessions.

outline.heading: Make up before next Ramadan
outline.gist: Missed days must be made up before the next Ramadan. Sisters who miss a week or the whole month through pregnancy or nursing often remember thirty days before; days still owed when Ramadan arrives must still be made up, plus a fidyah, which may be given to the poor in any country.

outline.heading: The major expiation, in order
outline.gist: Breaking the fast by intercourse requires the major expiation, in order: free a slave; if not, fast sixty consecutive days; if unable, feed sixty poor people.

outline.heading: Sixty days, or $1,200
outline.gist: He recently learned of someone who fell into this, fasted sixty consecutive days and benefited enormously. Feeding sixty means a full, satisfying meal each, about $20 today, so roughly $1,200. He teases couples who ignore each other all year and only find each other on a Ramadan afternoon.

outline.heading: Deliberate ejaculation
outline.gist: Far more common among young men is deliberate ejaculation. Most scholars do not require the major expiation for it, only repentance and a make-up day, though there is no harm in someone choosing to do it by analogy, as some young men have.

outline.heading: Deliberate eating, a major expiation too
outline.gist: All agree intercourse requires the major expiation; the schools are split over deliberate eating and drinking. He holds it deserves it even more, as when someone breaks his fast in a fit of anger: free a slave, fast two months or feed sixty, and the $1,200 will hurt.

outline.heading: The minor expiation and chronic illness
outline.gist: The minor expiation is feeding one poor person for each day, the fidyah of the verse. It is for chronic illness such as dialysis or diabetes; insulin under the skin does not break the fast in his view, but depending on the type of diabetes, fasting may put a patient in a coma.

outline.heading: Elderly diabetics in the emergency room
outline.gist: During his hospital years, elderly women with diabetes who insisted on fasting arrived late at night with dangerously low or high sugar. Advice goes in one ear and out the other; the best thing is a son who calls him to talk to his mother.

outline.heading: Six hundred dollars to feed the hungry
outline.gist: A chronically ill person simply multiplies: thirty meals at $20 is $600, paid at once to feed the poor. This masjid does not collect zakat or expiations, but many others run feeding programs, and half the Muslim world is hungry. It must go to feeding, not to building a hospital; charity covers those.

outline.heading: Not to your parents or children
outline.gist: Zakat cannot go to your parents or children, since it would return to you as inheritance. Pay the dues in their channels and give your family from your own money; even the Arabs of jahiliyyah were more generous than people who calculate exactly what they owe.

outline.heading: Why this masjid refuses zakat
outline.gist: Every year someone offers his company's zakat of seventy or a hundred thousand, though the masjid barely survives and its tent alone cost $20,000. He does not see it as permissible for masjids to take zakat, though others hold differently.

outline.heading: Zakat's prescribed channels
outline.gist: Zakat goes to its recipients: the poor, the needy and those who work on it. If you personally find the poor and distribute it you may keep at most a tenth, but not if you pass it to a charity. Most must go to the poor and needy; give as Allah ordered, then give from your own wealth. Cash given with the intention of feeding is fine.

outline.heading: Fidyah for the elderly
outline.gist: The elderly need not be ill: whoever has reached extreme old age may break the fast and pay fidyah, as in the fiqh of the elderly and of women past childbearing. Some scholars say a child with means should pay for a parent. There is no fixed age; it depends on custom and strength.

outline.heading: One fidyah per missed day
outline.gist: Whoever delays a make-up past the next Ramadan owes one fidyah per day, not one for every year it is delayed; sisters with fasts owed since 1998 need not bankrupt their husbands. They make up the days, and the delay is a sin requiring repentance, graver than the expiation.

outline.heading: Nursing and pregnant women
outline.gist: A pregnant or nursing woman may break her fast, but owes the minor expiation even if she makes the days up before next Ramadan: break, pay the fidyah right away, and make up the day.

outline.heading: A day no lifetime can replace
outline.gist: A Ramadan day broken without excuse cannot be made up by fasting a lifetime, as the Prophet said. You still fast a day in its place, but the reward lost cannot be recovered; with an excuse you lose nothing. That is how Allah honours the obligation. He lists again who owes the minor expiation.

outline.heading: Do not drink like a camel
outline.gist: Delay suhoor as the hadith says, but drinking huge amounts helps only if you have a hump; you just spend the day in the washroom. A few litres spread out is enough: one in the morning, one at iftar, one and a half at night, unless you are an athlete or have a condition.

outline.heading: Salt and sugar call for water
outline.gist: Salty snacks at suhoor will kill you by midday: salts and sugars draw water by osmosis, so the more of them you eat, the more you must drink. Keep suhoor moderate.

outline.heading: Suhoor for its blessing
outline.gist: Eat suhoor for the blessing the Prophet taught. His suhoor, like his iftar, was a few dates, water and perhaps milk; you need nothing more. He marvels at families cooking every dish for an hour and a half before Fajr.

outline.heading: Hasten iftar, delay suhoor: no extra zeal
outline.gist: Do not delay iftar. Adding unprescribed devotion is the essence of bid'ah: the fast is Fajr to Maghrib, not two hours either side, so take your last bite just before the adhan and break the fast at once. The Prophet commanded ease, not exaggeration.

outline.heading: Break on fresh dates
outline.gist: The sunnah is to break the fast on fresh dates, or dry dates if there are none, or water; other food is fine, but never a cigarette or a sin.

outline.heading: The dua at iftar
outline.gist: The fasting person's dua at iftar is not rejected. Whether you make it just before or just after breaking the fast is a verbal difference not worth arguing over.

outline.heading: Fast from sins too
outline.gist: Fasting from the lawful while cursing, backbiting, fighting, looking at and eating the forbidden makes no sense: whoever does not abandon false speech and acting on it, Allah has no need for him to leave his food and drink.

outline.heading: Young people, pray it in full
outline.gist: Not strictly fiqh of fasting, but pray tarawih in full, especially if you are young, in a masjid that completes the Quran, with a mushaf open. People queue for hours for a certificate, and back pain only seems to strike in tarawih, never at the dabke.

outline.heading: Leave with the imam
outline.gist: Getting into the habit young matters. In the Prophet's era leaving before the imam finished was a sign of hypocrisy; today someone with work in the morning may leave, but without an excuse stay to the end, the greatest reward of prayer in Ramadan.

outline.heading: The number carries no weight
outline.gist: Twenty, twelve, eight or forty-six: whoever thinks the number is a problem has not read fiqh, and the imams differed on it. What matters is how much Quran is recited. Insist on the Prophet's eight rak'ahs and we start at eight and finish at three.

outline.heading: The sunnah is a khatm
outline.gist: The Prophet recited what had been revealed many times over in Ramadan. Al-Nawawi in al-Majmu' says the sunnah is at least one khatm, and tarawih's sunnah ends with the khatm the imam intended. They pray ten plus three here, following two sound hadiths, from Zayd ibn Khalid in Muslim and Ibn Abbas in Bukhari.

outline.heading: Pray it in the masjid
outline.gist: The number lets people leave in time for work while hearing the whole Quran without exhausting rak'ahs. Home and masjid are both valid, but he prefers the masjid, since at home laziness wins the first time the father has a headache. Commit to a masjid that completes the Quran and come early.

outline.heading: Bound to the imam
outline.gist: Tarawih is named for the rest between its sets. Once you say Allahu akbar behind the imam you are bound until he finishes. Ibn Masud admitted he once intended something bad, to leave the Prophet in prayer, and the man who left Mu'adh's long Isha was said to have become a hypocrite.

outline.heading: Rest or sit, but do not leave
outline.gist: The imam stands straight up for the next set, but you may rest for two rak'ahs in your place or pray sitting, which earns reward. That is far better than praying four or six and walking out.

outline.heading: Zakat al-fitr in cash
outline.gist: People love to fight every year over paying zakat al-fitr in cash. The Hanafis allowed it long ago, and every school has a view permitting it; give a sa' of dates, barley or wheat, or cash, as you prefer. The matter is broad.

outline.heading: Give it about a week early
outline.gist: It must be paid before the Eid prayer, and may be paid days or a week before, after mid-month as the Shafi'is say, or from the start of Ramadan. He prefers about a week early so it reaches families in time for their children to enjoy Eid; it is roughly $15 to $20 a person.

outline.heading: For everyone you support, even the unborn
outline.gist: The provider pays for those he supports: wife, children, and parents if he supports them; a father may still pay for an independent son as extra good. It is also paid for a fetus past 120 days, when the soul is breathed in, as Imam Ahmad and others hold.

outline.heading: The Eid prayer: later is fine, one gathering
outline.gist: Go out to the Eid prayer with your family, outdoors. Eid al-Fitr may be delayed toward midday if that is easier for people. The sunnah is one gathering in one or two places, not sixty separate Eids; the Prophet took the whole town out with families and even their animals.

outline.heading: Outro

62:9.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓاْ إِذَا نُودِيَ لِلصَّلَوٰةِ مِن يَوۡمِ ٱلۡجُمُعَةِ فَٱسۡعَوۡاْ إِلَىٰ ذِكۡرِ ٱللَّهِ وَذَرُواْ ٱلۡبَيۡعَۚ ذَٰلِكُمۡ خَيۡرࣱ لَّكُمۡ إِن كُنتُمۡ تَعۡلَمُونَ
62:9.en: O you who have believed, when [the adhan] is called for the prayer on the day of Jumu'ah [Friday], then proceed to the remembrance of Allah and leave trade. That is better for you, if you only knew

62:10.ar: فَإِذَا قُضِيَتِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةُ فَٱنتَشِرُواْ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَٱبۡتَغُواْ مِن فَضۡلِ ٱللَّهِ وَٱذۡكُرُواْ ٱللَّهَ كَثِيرࣰ ا لَّعَلَّكُمۡ تُفۡلِحُونَ
62:10.en: And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse within the land and seek from the bounty of Allah, and remember Allah often that you may succeed

62:11.ar: وَإِذَا رَأَوۡاْ تِجَٰرَةً أَوۡ لَهۡوًا ٱنفَضُّوٓاْ إِلَيۡهَا وَتَرَكُوكَ قَآئِمࣰ اۚ قُلۡ مَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ خَيۡرࣱ مِّنَ ٱللَّهۡوِ وَمِنَ ٱلتِّجَٰرَةِۚ وَٱللَّهُ خَيۡرُ ٱلرَّٰزِقِينَ
62:11.en: But when they saw a transaction or a diversion, [O Muhammad], they rushed to it and left you standing. Say, "What is with Allah is better than diversion and than a transaction, and Allah is the best of providers

62:5.ar: مَثَلُ ٱلَّذِينَ حُمِّلُواْ ٱلتَّوۡرَىٰةَ ثُمَّ لَمۡ يَحۡمِلُوهَا كَمَثَلِ ٱلۡحِمَارِ يَحۡمِلُ أَسۡفَارَۢاۚ بِئۡسَ مَثَلُ ٱلۡقَوۡمِ ٱلَّذِينَ كَذَّبُواْ بِـَٔايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِۚ وَٱللَّهُ لَا يَهۡدِي ٱلۡقَوۡمَ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
62:5.en: The example of those who were entrusted with the Torah and then did not take it on is like that of a donkey who carries volumes [of books]. Wretched is the example of the people who deny the signs of Allah. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people

62:6.ar: قُلۡ يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ هَادُوٓاْ إِن زَعَمۡتُمۡ أَنَّكُمۡ أَوۡلِيَآءُ لِلَّهِ مِن دُونِ ٱلنَّاسِ فَتَمَنَّوُاْ ٱلۡمَوۡتَ إِن كُنتُمۡ صَٰدِقِينَ
62:6.en: Say, "O you who are Jews, if you claim that you are allies of Allah, excluding the [other] people, then wish for death, if you should be truthful

62:7.ar: وَلَا يَتَمَنَّوۡنَهُۥٓ أَبَدَۢا بِمَا قَدَّمَتۡ أَيۡدِيهِمۡۚ وَٱللَّهُ عَلِيمُۢ بِٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
62:7.en: But they will not wish for it, ever, because of what their hands have put forth. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers

62:8.ar: قُلۡ إِنَّ ٱلۡمَوۡتَ ٱلَّذِي تَفِرُّونَ مِنۡهُ فَإِنَّهُۥ مُلَٰقِيكُمۡۖ ثُمَّ تُرَدُّونَ إِلَىٰ عَٰلِمِ ٱلۡغَيۡبِ وَٱلشَّهَٰدَةِ فَيُنَبِّئُكُم بِمَا كُنتُمۡ تَعۡمَلُونَ
62:8.en: Say, "Indeed, the death from which you flee - indeed, it will meet you. Then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you about what you used to do

Rbqi7mhnXTI.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Jumuah 62:9-11 (Part 4)
Rbqi7mhnXTI.one_line: The closing verses of Al-Jumuah are addressed to the attendees: hasten to Jumuah, follow and question your leadership, and never leave the khatib standing alone.
Rbqi7mhnXTI.summary: Closing Surat Al-Jumuah, he first restates his reading of the surah in a long review: Jumuah is the leadership system Allah built into the religion. Muslims have neutralized it by turning the khatib into a salaried employee of a board with no vision of his own. The person on the minbar should either be the community's leader or speak openly on that leader's behalf. The earlier verses addressed the khatib. These final three address the congregation, whose duty is to be willing to be led, to follow, to give feedback and to hold leaders accountable. Western masjids have no excuse, because no regime scripts their sermons. On 62:9 he stresses that Jumuah is obligatory for resident men, criticizes the laxity that followed Covid, and cites the severe hadith on missing it. He explains the call to hasten and to leave all trade, including the trade of selling oneself. On 62:10 he says the masjid is not a place to stay: go out, seek Allah's bounty, and act on what you learned while remembering Him. On 62:11 he tells the story of the caravan that drew people away while the Prophet stood on the minbar. He reads 'standing' as carrying a burden alone, and says no imam can carry the religion by himself.

outline.heading: Opening
A simple surah: Jumuah organizes the ummah
outline.gist: The surah organizes leadership simply: each week the leader stands on the minbar, says what comes next and revises the plan, and the men who attend inform their families.

outline.heading: Neutralized, but still alive
outline.gist: Muslims have neutralized Jumuah almost everywhere, yet reviving it would change their state quickly because it still exists and even those far from Allah attend. It only needs a worthy message from someone with authority to lead; he himself has no wish to lead.

outline.heading: The leader, or someone clearly speaking for him
outline.gist: As a young man he gave khutbahs for his elderly teacher, who still led the community. A khatib employed by a board to hit its milestones is a puppet with no vision; today's Jumuah is neither the leader nor his spokesman, just a lecture on steroids.

outline.heading: A community that meets weekly cannot fail
outline.gist: Once people stop finding benefit they stop coming, yet a community whose leader tells it every week where it is going, and which follows up and gives feedback, can hardly fail.

outline.heading: The first page addressed the khatib
outline.gist: The earlier verses chastise the speaker: if he fails to teach responsibility instead of favour and to remind people of death, the congregation becomes a donkey carrying books. The final verses address the attendees.

outline.heading: Being willing to be led
outline.gist: Attendees are part of the fabric of Jumuah: it needs someone to lead and people willing to be led. That does not mean surrendering autonomy, and no one is obeyed in disobedience to Allah.

outline.heading: Following only your own direction makes you the leader
outline.gist: Walking behind a leader only when he goes your way is not followship. Trust a reasoned direction, and if it proves wrong the weekly Jumuah will correct it; anything beats being a headless chicken.

outline.heading: Poor followers are part of the problem
outline.gist: He calls himself a decorated complainer. Blame imams and boards all you like, but a poor follower is part of the problem; at work you are not always the leader either, and that lessens no one.

outline.heading: Follow, give feedback, hold accountable: the Prophet's weekly loop
outline.gist: Jumuah is a two-way road: one person speaks, everyone listens, and feedback comes through the week so the next khutbah responds to it. That loop is how the Prophet grew his community.

outline.heading: No regime scripts our khutbahs
outline.gist: In Syria or Egypt a totalitarian regime hands the imam a script he cannot leave. Here masajid have autonomy, so the only barrier to proper leadership is ourselves.

outline.heading: Large US masajid and a clear structure
outline.gist: Some very large American masajid thrive because everyone, the imam included, knows who makes the calls. An imam need not lead, only know who his leader is so he can move people in that direction.

outline.heading: Reciting 62:9-11, and the connecting hamza
outline.gist: He introduces the final passage as addressed to attendees and followers, recites it, and notes that a connecting hamza is pronounced only when starting from it and drops in continuous reading.

outline.heading: The first call to the believers
outline.gist: Until now the surah did not address the believers; it described Allah's attributes, the purpose of prophets and what happens when leaders fail. This passage is for the attendee.

outline.heading: Favoured or responsible?
outline.gist: Feeling favoured by Allah and feeling responsible to Him are easily confused but opposite: the first leads to rock bottom, the second motivates you to use what you were given.

outline.heading: When the call is made on Friday
outline.gist: The call meant is the Friday prayer, which the Prophet always held in place of Dhuhr; the verse need not say so because his practice settles it.

outline.heading: No adhan in the street: plan for Jumuah
outline.gist: Back home you hear the adhan and close your shop. Here you must set reminders, arrange time with your employer, find the nearest Jumuah and transport, and that extra effort is obligatory.

outline.heading: An obligation for men, despite the post-COVID slide
outline.gist: After COVID young men grew lax about Jumuah. It is optional for women but mandatory for every resident man, with no exception but illness or travel.

outline.heading: Whatever the quality of the khutbah
outline.gist: A surgeon mid-operation or a pilot may be excused, but otherwise you attend even if the khatib speaks Klingon to people from Mars: praise Allah, pray and leave.

outline.heading: The threat to burn houses
outline.gist: The Prophet said he had intended to have wood gathered and burn the houses of Muslim men who stay away from Jumuah; such strict language from him signals something major.

outline.heading: Harsh warnings mark a system, not only a ritual
outline.gist: Whoever misses three in a row without excuse has his heart turned away. Like zakah, the ummah's financial backbone that Abu Bakr fought to keep, Jumuah is a leadership system, and abandoning it rips the ummah's fabric.

outline.heading: Hasten with tunnel vision
outline.gist: Fas'aw means moving quickly and forcefully, dropping everything with tunnel vision toward the remembrance of Allah, where you hear what He wants from you and for you.

outline.heading: Remembering Allah as a community
outline.gist: An individual can worship alone, but a community praises Allah by knowing where it is going, picking up its pace, caring for its vulnerable and solving its acute and chronic problems.

outline.heading: Leave all selling, including selling yourself
outline.gist: Every person goes out each morning selling himself, freeing or ruining himself. Leave every transaction, whether goods, tuition or hours for a paycheck.

outline.heading: Better for you, if you knew
outline.gist: Nothing is more valuable than having Jumuah. At 38 he has spent twenty years trying to work out how to fix it, when the solution is already built in.

outline.heading: Disperse and seek Allah's bounty
outline.gist: Allah fills the masjid on Friday because He calls the people. When the prayer ends, go out: masajid are not places to stay all day, and there is work to do while remembering Allah much.

outline.heading: Take the week's lesson out with you
outline.gist: Do not seek your livelihood and forget Allah until next Friday; carry the remembrance you were given and act on what you learned that week.

outline.heading: That you may succeed, as a community
outline.gist: Success comes when people attend faithfully, hear a direction from the minbar, and spend the week pursuing it while remembering Allah.

outline.heading: A verse that made his teachers weep
outline.gist: Some of his teachers could not recite this verse without tears. When people see a profitable deal or some amusement, lesser priorities than Jumuah, they rush toward it.

outline.heading: The caravan during the khutbah
outline.gist: Infaddu means pushing and shoving to get out. Early in Medina a trading caravan arrived while the Prophet was on the minbar, and because goods were scarce people ran out to buy, leaving him standing; the verse came down about this.

outline.heading: Standing: carrying the burden alone
outline.gist: Qa'im in the Quran means taking a stand and carrying its burden, not just being upright, so they left him carrying the responsibility alone.

outline.heading: What is with Allah is better
outline.gist: What Allah holds for you through this system beats any amusement or deal, and He is the best of providers, so missing the first bid is no loss. Do not leave the speaker standing while you walk out.

outline.heading: No khatib can carry the deen alone
outline.gist: If the person on the minbar carries the religion alone it is a disaster; everyone must share the ownership. The Prophet did not stop the khutbah to follow them, so if the speaker is still speaking you are still listening.

outline.heading: Jumuah as a symbolic commitment
outline.gist: Attending is a symbolic commitment to the nation and its leadership. The argument is hard to make when Jumuah has become a token, yet in Islam you cannot stop your part because others do theirs badly.

outline.heading: In Islam you always do your part
outline.gist: Attend whether the imam is good or bad or shouts a lot, look for better if you can, and attend anyway if you cannot; then hold leaders accountable for offering direction worth following.

outline.heading: Replace khatibs who give no direction

JW9TPthJdbg.title: Ramadan Prep: The Bounties of Ramadan
JW9TPthJdbg.one_line: The Prophet's pre-Ramadan sermon explained, then five bounties to aim for: forgiveness, freedom from the Fire, immense reward, Laylat al-Qadr and answered dua.
JW9TPthJdbg.summary: He explains the long narration of the Prophet's sermon before Ramadan, noting that scholars dispute its chain but accept its meaning. Each phrase becomes a lesson: a voluntary deed in Ramadan equals an obligation, and nothing outweighs an obligation; it is the month of patience, rewarded with Paradise without reckoning, where patience means holding a high standard rather than having a hard life; the month of empathy, since hunger teaches what the poor feel, as the Prophet and companions bound stones to their stomachs; provision grows because appreciation grows, which he ties to watching people starved on screens while the ummah fails its duty; and feeding the fasting was meant first for those with nothing. He then sets out five bounties to aim for. Forgiveness of sins through fasting, night prayer and Laylat al-Qadr offers a clean slate. Freedom from the Fire is granted every night on merit, the moment the Prophet sought most. Fasting's reward is beyond numbers, but only if one avoids haram while abstaining from halal. Laylat al-Qadr teaches quality over quantity, centres on the Quran and is spoiled by quarrels. The fasting person's dua is answered, so he urges people to learn to speak to Allah humbly and without formality.

outline.heading: Opening
Know the bounties so you have a target
outline.gist: Ramadan brings a closeness and serenity found at no other time; knowing its five bounties gives you something to aim for all month.

outline.heading: The Prophet's sermon before Ramadan
outline.gist: The narration's chain is disputed but its meaning is accepted by scholars and his teachers; the Prophet stood on the minbar days before Ramadan, and Arabs distinguished such an oration from a seated talk.

outline.heading: A great month with a night of a thousand months
outline.gist: Fasting its days is obligatory, praying its nights voluntary, and any good deed in it counts as an obligation done elsewhere.

outline.heading: Why equalling an obligation matters
outline.gist: All voluntary deeds ever done do not equal one obligation, and a missed obligation's reward is never recovered; in Ramadan one obligation counts as seventy.

outline.heading: The month of patience: Paradise without reckoning
outline.gist: Standing before Allah to account for youth, wealth and time is the hardest moment of existence; the patient are spared it entirely.

outline.heading: What patience really means
outline.gist: Patience is not having a hard life but setting a high standard and persevering toward it; Ramadan is hard by design and its reward is Paradise.

outline.heading: The month of empathy
outline.gist: Fasting voluntarily teaches what involuntary hunger feels like, just as recovered addicts make the best counsellors.

outline.heading: Months without a cooking fire
outline.gist: The Prophet's household went months on dates and water; companions bound stones to their stomachs, which shrinks the stomach's pouch and dulls hunger, as gastric bypass does.

outline.heading: One stone each, and the Prophet's two
outline.gist: Three hungry young men showed the Prophet the stones on their bellies; he smiled and showed two on his own.

outline.heading: Do not spend Ramadan feeling sorry for yourself
outline.gist: You will be fine at sunset; let the month strengthen empathy for those who will not, so that you give more.

outline.heading: Provision increases through appreciation
outline.gist: His bank balance never grew in Ramadan; what grows is gratitude, as hunger makes an old car and a modest income look like plenty.

outline.heading: Starvation broadcast on our screens
outline.gist: There is money to film people starving to death but not to feed them; the brutality against the people of the Holy Land should make this Ramadan a turning point.

outline.heading: The ummah has not done its job
outline.gist: Such disregard for Muslim life shows Muslims have neglected their purpose and responsibilities; feel it as you break a fast others cannot.

outline.heading: Entitled children and entitled servants
outline.gist: Parents are worn out by children who always want more; Allah sees us the same way, and we forget that what we have could be much less.

outline.heading: Feeding the fasting person
outline.gist: Whoever gives iftar earns the faster's reward; family iftars are good, but the Prophet meant first those who could not otherwise break their fast; the month runs from mercy to forgiveness to freedom from the Fire.

outline.heading: Bounty one: forgiveness of sins
outline.gist: Believers feel the weight of their shortcomings rather than comparing themselves with the public, so a wiped slate matters most to them.

outline.heading: Fasting with faith and hope of reward
outline.gist: Whoever fasts Ramadan out of faith and seeking reward has his past sins forgiven.

outline.heading: Night prayer, Laylat al-Qadr and a greyed-out record
outline.gist: Standing its nights or Laylat al-Qadr also forgives past sins; imagine your record with the bad deeds still there but stamped forgiven.

outline.heading: Allah offers a fresh start
outline.gist: It is as if Allah says let us begin again; He loves to forgive where people do not, so missing it is a real loss.

outline.heading: Three 'ameens' on the minbar
outline.gist: Jibril prayed against whoever reaches Ramadan and is not forgiven; with so many routes to forgiveness, missing them takes effort.

outline.heading: Bounty two: freedom from the Fire
outline.gist: Like freeing a slave, Allah breaks the chain that binds a person to Hell, and He frees people every night of Ramadan.

outline.heading: Not a lottery but merit
outline.gist: More are freed in the last ten nights, and being chosen outweighs graduation, marriage, a first child or a dream promotion.

outline.heading: A freedom never revoked
outline.gist: Once granted it is never taken back; you may still sin, but you will always find your way back to Allah and your end will be good.

outline.heading: What the Prophet asked for most
outline.gist: Most of his supplications at the end of Ramadan, rich in glorifying Allah, centred on this; what a loss to pass a Ramadan without it.

outline.heading: Hell paraded on the Day of Judgement
outline.gist: Hell is dragged out by 70,000 reins each held by 70,000 angels, straining to devour; knees buckle and no one dares look straight at it.

outline.heading: Bring your best: there is no nepotism
outline.gist: The freed are far from all of it because they gave their all one night in Ramadan; it is granted on merit.

outline.heading: Bounty three: reward beyond measure
outline.gist: Beyond the multiplied deeds, Allah says every deed has a set reward except fasting, which is His and which He rewards Himself.

outline.heading: The blank line on the billboard
outline.gist: Scanning the reward values for your deeds you find none for fasting, because Allah will reward it personally; a modest effort for us is a great deal to Him.

outline.heading: The red line moves in Ramadan
outline.gist: Fasting pushes you back from even halal food, drink and marital relations, so fighting, cursing or gossiping while fasting makes no sense.

outline.heading: Fasting that yields only hunger
outline.gist: Many get nothing from fasting but hunger and nothing from night prayer but fatigue, because they lacked intention and focus.

outline.heading: Bounty four: Laylat al-Qadr, quality over quantity
outline.gist: Surah al-Qadr came about a decade before fasting was prescribed, teaching that a night can outweigh a thousand months, about 82 years, a whole lifetime.

outline.heading: The Prophet's search and the quarrel
outline.gist: He secluded himself in the first, middle and last ten nights until told it lay in the last ten, then forgot its date while reconciling two men fighting outside the masjid.

outline.heading: Do not spoil it with disputes
outline.gist: The lesson is not to ruin the night by harming people or dividing the community; seek it in the odd nights, counted from the start or the end.

outline.heading: Dedicate all ten nights
outline.gist: Scholars reject betting only on the 27th; it is hidden so we commit to all ten, and a single prostration that night could weigh like 82 years.

outline.heading: The night is about the Quran
outline.gist: It marks the first revelation; Umm Ayman wept that revelation had ended, but each year Jibril descends with the angels to see the Quran alive in the hearts of the ummah.

outline.heading: Peace until dawn
outline.gist: Allah grants peace to all creation that night, so a quarrel ruins it; guard your behaviour in the last ten.

outline.heading: Bounty five: the fasting person's dua
outline.gist: Its acceptance means a response: what you asked, something better later, harm removed, sins forgiven or rank raised, while some duas are thrown back.

outline.heading: Prepare your dua in advance
outline.gist: Use the free dua at iftar; earlier generations prepared and memorised their Ramadan duas months ahead so they were ready in every prostration.

outline.heading: Islam is learning to speak to Allah
outline.gist: Islam teaches who Allah is and how to communicate with Him, a relationship unlike any other we have.

outline.heading: Come without titles
outline.gist: Dua is not a formal interview; in prostration you put your face in the dirt, so come as a weak, scared creature without your degrees or bank balance.

outline.heading: The dua exercise
outline.gist: Say every memorised dua, then sit again and make a second dua without repeating a single word, to learn to speak unmasked.

outline.heading: 2:186: no middleman
outline.gist: When asked about Allah, the verse drops the usual 'say' and Allah answers directly that He is near and responds.

outline.heading: The gates of Heaven open
outline.gist: Ramadan's different feel, impossible to replicate, is because Heaven's gates are open and Hell's are shut.

outline.heading: Devils chained: the sin is yours
outline.gist: With the devils chained, any sin in Ramadan comes from your own nafs, a lesson in telling internal from external sources of sin.

outline.heading: Allah calls the hearts
outline.gist: A caller invites seekers of good to come forward; Allah draws crowds no programme could, and the truly deprived is the one who misses Ramadan's mercy.

9:91.ar: لَّيۡسَ عَلَى ٱلضُّعَفَآءِ وَلَا عَلَى ٱلۡمَرۡضَىٰ وَلَا عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ لَا يَجِدُونَ مَا يُنفِقُونَ حَرَجٌ إِذَا نَصَحُواْ لِلَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِۦۚ مَا عَلَى ٱلۡمُحۡسِنِينَ مِن سَبِيلࣲۚ وَٱللَّهُ غَفُورࣱ رَّحِيمࣱ‏
9:91.en: There is not upon the weak or upon the ill or upon those who do not find anything to spend any discomfort when they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger. There is not upon the doers of good any cause [for blame]. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful

9:92.ar: وَلَا عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ إِذَا مَآ أَتَوۡكَ لِتَحۡمِلَهُمۡ قُلۡتَ لَآ أَجِدُ مَآ أَحۡمِلُكُمۡ عَلَيۡهِ تَوَلَّواْ وَّأَعۡيُنُهُمۡ تَفِيضُ مِنَ ٱلدَّمۡعِ حَزَنًا أَلَّا يَجِدُواْ مَا يُنفِقُونَ
9:92.en: Nor [is there blame] upon those who, when they came to you that you might give them mounts, you said, "I can find nothing for you to ride upon." They turned back while their eyes overflowed with tears out of grief that they could not find something to spend [for the cause of Allah]

9:93.ar: ۞إِنَّمَا ٱلسَّبِيلُ عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ يَسۡتَـٔۡذِنُونَكَ وَهُمۡ أَغۡنِيَآءُۚ رَضُواْ بِأَن يَكُونُواْ مَعَ ٱلۡخَوَالِفِ وَطَبَعَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِمۡ فَهُمۡ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ
9:93.en: The cause [for blame] is only upon those who ask permission of you while they are rich. They are satisfied to be with those who stay behind, and Allah has sealed over their hearts, so they do not know

9:94.ar: يَعۡتَذِرُونَ إِلَيۡكُمۡ إِذَا رَجَعۡتُمۡ إِلَيۡهِمۡۚ قُل لَّا تَعۡتَذِرُواْ لَن نُّؤۡمِنَ لَكُمۡ قَدۡ نَبَّأَنَا ٱللَّهُ مِنۡ أَخۡبَارِكُمۡۚ وَسَيَرَى ٱللَّهُ عَمَلَكُمۡ وَرَسُولُهُۥ ثُمَّ تُرَدُّونَ إِلَىٰ عَٰلِمِ ٱلۡغَيۡبِ وَٱلشَّهَٰدَةِ فَيُنَبِّئُكُم بِمَا كُنتُمۡ تَعۡمَلُونَ
9:94.en: They will make excuses to you when you have returned to them. Say, "Make no excuse - never will we believe you. Allah has already informed us of your news. And Allah will observe your deeds, and [so will] His Messenger; then you will be taken back to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do

9:95.ar: سَيَحۡلِفُونَ بِٱللَّهِ لَكُمۡ إِذَا ٱنقَلَبۡتُمۡ إِلَيۡهِمۡ لِتُعۡرِضُواْ عَنۡهُمۡۖ فَأَعۡرِضُواْ عَنۡهُمۡۖ إِنَّهُمۡ رِجۡسࣱۖ وَمَأۡوَىٰهُمۡ جَهَنَّمُ جَزَآءَۢ بِمَا كَانُواْ يَكۡسِبُونَ
9:95.en: They will swear by Allah to you when you return to them that you would leave them alone. So leave them alone; indeed they are evil; and their refuge is Hell as recompense for what they had been earning

9:96.ar: يَحۡلِفُونَ لَكُمۡ لِتَرۡضَوۡاْ عَنۡهُمۡۖ فَإِن تَرۡضَوۡاْ عَنۡهُمۡ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَرۡضَىٰ عَنِ ٱلۡقَوۡمِ ٱلۡفَٰسِقِينَ
9:96.en: They swear to you so that you might be satisfied with them. But if you should be satisfied with them - indeed, Allah is not satisfied with a defiantly disobedient people

9:117.ar: لَّقَد تَّابَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَى ٱلنَّبِيِّ وَٱلۡمُهَٰجِرِينَ وَٱلۡأَنصَارِ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱتَّبَعُوهُ فِي سَاعَةِ ٱلۡعُسۡرَةِ مِنۢ بَعۡدِ مَا كَادَ يَزِيغُ قُلُوبُ فَرِيقࣲ مِّنۡهُمۡ ثُمَّ تَابَ عَلَيۡهِمۡۚ إِنَّهُۥ بِهِمۡ رَءُوفࣱ رَّحِيمࣱ‏
9:117.en: Allah has already forgiven the Prophet and the Muhajireen and the Ansar who followed him in the hour of difficulty after the hearts of a party of them had almost inclined [to doubt], and then He forgave them. Indeed, He was to them Kind and Merciful

9:118.ar: وَعَلَى ٱلثَّلَٰثَةِ ٱلَّذِينَ خُلِّفُواْ حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَا ضَاقَتۡ عَلَيۡهِمُ ٱلۡأَرۡضُ بِمَا رَحُبَتۡ وَضَاقَتۡ عَلَيۡهِمۡ أَنفُسُهُمۡ وَظَنُّوٓاْ أَن لَّا مَلۡجَأَ مِنَ ٱللَّهِ إِلَّآ إِلَيۡهِ ثُمَّ تَابَ عَلَيۡهِمۡ لِيَتُوبُوٓاْۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ هُوَ ٱلتَّوَّابُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ

qFtXNE8yRd4.title: The Expedition of Tabuk and the Story of Ka'b ibn Malik
qFtXNE8yRd4.one_line: Ka'b ibn Malik's staying back from Tabuk, his honesty and fifty-day boycott, and what At-Tawbah teaches about earning a place with the Prophet.
qFtXNE8yRd4.summary: Framed as preparation for Ramadan, he tells the story of Ka'b ibn Malik, mostly in Ka'b's own words from his long narration, alongside the verses of At-Tawbah. He sets the scene: the Prophet openly declared a long march north against Roman-allied forces in the August heat at harvest time, and everyone had to carry his own provisions. The weak and the poor were excused, but the wealthy who sought permission were not. Ka'b, a famous poet who had lost his court income on becoming Muslim, finally had the means to go, yet kept putting it off until it was too late. When the army returned and others offered false excuses, he chose to tell the truth, admitting he simply stayed back for his own interests. He stresses that honesty is not optional, that the hypocrites were never exposed or punished in this life, and that belonging to the Prophet's community brings more accountability. He then narrates the fifty-day boycott, the Prophet looking away, the earth closing in, the Ghassanid king's offer that Ka'b burned, and the joy of forgiveness. The lesson is that At-Tawbah calls for repentance from self-interest when the ummah needs us, that a place near the Prophet must be earned, and that the only refuge from Allah is Allah.

outline.heading: At-Tawbah and the 'hour of difficulty'
outline.gist: He picks a story meant to shape the approach to Ramadan; the Quran names the expedition the hour of difficulty, and Ka'b's own long narration is worth reading in full.

outline.heading: Why the Prophet named Tabuk openly
outline.gist: Unlike other campaigns he named the destination, marching north to meet Roman-allied Arab forces outside Arab lands rather than wait for them to come to Madinah.

outline.heading: No blame on the weak, the ill and the poor
outline.gist: It was August at date harvest, people were poor, and the journey demanded camels, shoes and food; those without means were excused.

outline.heading: Everyone carries his own weight
outline.gist: No one could go expecting others to feed him; those who could not afford it left in tears, and the story is about not staying back out of self-interest.

outline.heading: The rich who asked to stay behind
outline.gist: The blame falls on the wealthy who sought permission; with no roll call, staying back went unnoticed unless revelation exposed it.

outline.heading: Ka'b: never wealthier than then
outline.gist: Ka'b begins by saying he had never been better off than at the time of Tabuk.

outline.heading: Ka'b the poet of the Prophet
outline.gist: An early Ansari Muslim and celebrated poet, he was one of the Prophet's three poets who answered Quraysh's propaganda.

outline.heading: Poetry as the news and record of its age
outline.gist: Poems documented battles and spread news across Arabia, which is why early seerah books are full of poetry.

outline.heading: Why a famous poet had little money
outline.gist: Islam cut him off from the patronage of kings, leaving him dependent on selling his dates at the end of August.

outline.heading: 'Tomorrow I'll prepare': putting it off
outline.gist: He had two camels, the ideal case, but kept delaying each day until the army was too far ahead to catch.

outline.heading: Left among the excused and the hypocrites
outline.gist: Walking through Madinah he saw only the genuinely excused and known hypocrites, and himself among them.

outline.heading: A companion defends his absent brother
outline.gist: When someone mocked Ka'b on the road, a companion defended him; we owe our brothers good assumptions without needing reasons.

outline.heading: The Prophet receives the excuses
outline.gist: Returning after fifty days, he sat in the masjid and accepted people's excuses without demanding proof, praying for them even though most were lying.

outline.heading: Ka'b's turn and the displeased smile
outline.gist: Ka'b resolved to be truthful; the Prophet smiled at him in a way that showed displeasure and asked about his camels.

outline.heading: 'I have no excuse'
outline.gist: A master of words, he refused to talk his way out, fearing Allah would expose a lie, and admitted he stayed back for his own interest.

outline.heading: The surah of repentance from self-interest
outline.gist: We all need to repent from being preoccupied with our own lives when the ummah needs our commitment.

outline.heading: Honesty is not optional
outline.gist: Truthfulness earns no extra points; it is required. The Prophet said Ka'b had told the truth and sent him to await Allah's decision.

outline.heading: The liars were never exposed
outline.gist: Hypocrites were never called out or punished in this life; their oaths are for show, and Allah is not pleased with them.

outline.heading: Belonging to the ummah carries a price
outline.gist: Those who truly belong are tested and held to account more, and being counted among the Prophet's people is worth that price.

outline.heading: Pressure to recant, and seventy prayers for forgiveness
outline.gist: His clan urged him to make up an excuse; the Prophet prayed for the liars, yet Allah said even seventy prayers would not forgive them.

outline.heading: Two companions of Badr in the same position
outline.gist: Two righteous men had done the same, which steadied him; he explains he had attended every battle and valued the pledge of Aqabah above Badr.

outline.heading: The boycott and the Prophet looking away
outline.gist: No one was to speak to the three for fifty days; what hurt Ka'b most was the Prophet glancing at him in prayer and looking away.

outline.heading: The earth closes in
outline.gist: Even his beloved cousin would not answer whether Ka'b loved Allah and His Messenger, and the vast earth felt narrow.

outline.heading: Separated from their wives
outline.gist: On the fortieth day they were told to keep away from their wives, adding to their grief.

outline.heading: The Ghassanid king's offer
outline.gist: A letter invited him to the king's court with honour; recognising it as a test, he burned it rather than abandon the Prophet.

outline.heading: The good news and the best day of his life
outline.gist: On the fiftieth day the news of forgiveness came; Talhah embraced him and the Prophet, face shining, called it the best day since he was born.

outline.heading: Allah turned to the Prophet and those who followed him
outline.gist: Allah accepted the repentance of all who followed in the hour of difficulty, even those whose hearts nearly wavered.

outline.heading: The three who were held back, and earning your place
outline.gist: 'Left behind' means made to wait for judgment, setting the truthful apart from the liars; a place in the Prophet's nation must be earned.

outline.heading: Sitting under the Prophet's garment
outline.gist: Ka'b sitting under the Prophet's cloak symbolises where we hope to be, a place that has to be earned.

outline.heading: The ummah still needs you
outline.gist: The Prophet is not physically here but the story is the same: we cannot put self-interest before the work he left us.

outline.heading: No refuge from Allah except in Him; be with the truthful
outline.gist: They realised the only escape from Allah is to Him; after the command to be with the truthful, Ka'b never lied again.

outline.heading: Outro

Jy6D9VP0myA.title: The Intention Behind Ramadan
Jy6D9VP0myA.one_line: Before planning Ramadan, set the intention: let it be the turning point that makes you someone who changes the ummah's course.
Jy6D9VP0myA.summary: A pre-Ramadan khutbah delivered while Gaza is being systematically starved. He opens with Ramadan as the month in which Allah calls hearts back, citing the narration of the month of barakah and the Prophet's three 'ameens' on the minbar, including the one against whoever lives through Ramadan without being forgiven. He then turns to Gaza and to three historical catastrophes: the Qarmatian massacre in Makkah and theft of the Black Stone, the Crusader capture of Jerusalem, and the Mongol sack of Baghdad. Each was reversed a generation or two later, often in Ramadan, once a new generation grew up refusing to accept the situation. His point is that this is not the worst the ummah has seen, so people should stop speculating about the end of time and ask what they are building for the next forty years. Responding to people who asked him to be more optimistic, he says his job is to sound an alarm, not a gentle reminder. Everyone will be asked what they did about what they witnessed. In the second khutbah he makes intention the first step of any Ramadan plan: decide why this Ramadan must change you. He ends by criticizing the community's fading advocacy and asks people to renew it as part of their Ramadan intention.

outline.heading: Opening
Nothing unites us like Ramadan
outline.gist: The fasting verse will open khutbahs all over the world for the coming weeks. Nothing unites the ummah like Ramadan, with Hajj a near second: a yearly chance to set things right and draw closer to Allah.

outline.heading: The King of hearts calls His servants
outline.gist: Anyone who works in a masjid in Ramadan sees faces never seen before filling it all month. That is not the masjid's doing: the King of hearts calls the hearts of His servants and they come.

outline.heading: A month of barakah
outline.gist: Ramadan has come to you, a month of barakah in which Allah covers you with mercy, forgives sins and answers dua, so show Him the best of yourselves; the wretched one is deprived of Allah's mercy in it. Then the Prophet climbed the three steps of the minbar saying ameen at each.

outline.heading: Three ameens: humiliated is the one not forgiven
outline.gist: Jibril made three duas; one was against whoever lives through Ramadan without being forgiven: may his nose be rubbed in the dust. You would have to work hard not to be forgiven in Ramadan.

outline.heading: Gaza is being starved
outline.gist: People in one of the richest regions on earth are being systematically starved after being ethnically cleansed, gunned down as they approach food trucks for their children, while the politicians we voted in support it. They will be shut out of the community until they admit the atrocities they backed.

outline.heading: The Qarmatians and the Black Stone
outline.gist: How bad can it get? In 317 AH the leader of an oppressive regime in eastern Arabia raided Makkah during Hajj, killed pilgrims in their thousands until the precinct of the Kaaba ran with blood, damaged the Kaaba and stole the Black Stone, holding it for 22 years before Muslims recovered it.

outline.heading: The Crusaders in Jerusalem
outline.gist: The Crusaders took the Holy Land, murdering Muslims and Jews, burning the masjid and turning it into a stable, and held it and parts of Lebanon, Jordan and Syria for decades until 583, in Ramadan, when it was retaken and Christians, Jews and Muslims could pray there again.

outline.heading: The Mongols in Baghdad
outline.gist: Less than a century later the Mongols burned Baghdad, killed everyone and threw the books of the greatest library on earth into the rivers until they ran red with blood and blue with ink. A couple of decades later, in 658 and again in Ramadan, they were driven back.

outline.heading: This is not the worst we have seen
outline.gist: We have always rebounded. This is not the end of time, not even close; your job is not to worry about when it comes but to know where you stand on your ummah's historical curve and what it needs from you. What were Hajj and Ramadan like in 318?

outline.heading: Every era thought it was Armageddon
outline.gist: Scholars of those eras wrote that the end was near, and it did not come in 583, 658, 1123, 1348 or today. The ummah is still large and full of people who care; despite his pessimism, it has rebounded from far worse.

outline.heading: A generation later, Ramadan was the spark
outline.gist: Most of these reversals came in Ramadan, a generation or two later, because the generation that suffered the catastrophe did not care enough; the next one grew up, refused to accept it and turned things around, as the Prophet gave a voice to the oppressed.

outline.heading: One spark from London, Ontario
outline.gist: Not a call for violence, but for each person to believe they will have an impact on the ummah's future. Even in a small city most people have never heard of, one person, or a hundred, can be one of the sparks that changes its history.

outline.heading: Work on what you can control
outline.gist: Believe it and be willing to work for it. Do not waste time on what you cannot control; what we see now was set in motion generations ago by people who stopped caring. The question is what you can do so it does not continue or happen again.

outline.heading: Asked to be more optimistic
outline.gist: What the next forty years look like depends on how we live now. Three people in one week asked him to be more optimistic; he would not be doing what he does if he did not believe to his core that this ummah can turn things around.

outline.heading: An alarm, not a gentle reminder
outline.gist: But at this point on the curve he is not a soft wake-up tone; he is here to sound an alarm that raises your heart rate and leaves you upset with yourself, as he is. Change cannot be slow and gradual: it has to be immediate, radical and huge.

outline.heading: You will be asked about what you witnessed
outline.gist: He has no stake in whether people listen; he knows his path. You will be asked not only about salah, zakah and family but about what you witnessed as part of this ummah and how you responded. 'I did nothing' is exactly the problem.

outline.heading: Aim higher: restore the truth
outline.gist: Where is the effect of witnessing tyranny and persecution on your life? Aim beyond Gaza and Palestine, for the ummah and for Allah, who created all this with truth: as long as falsehood prevails things will fail, and your job is to restore the truth and live it.

outline.heading: Every real tawbah story happens in Ramadan
outline.gist: He knows of no real story of repentance outside Ramadan: the decision that enough is enough, no longer a bystander focused on small things, happens in it, which is why those battles were won in it too.

outline.heading: Interlude
Intention first: why will you fast?
outline.gist: Number one in any Ramadan plan is intention: why you fast, pray and take part, beyond the ritual of hunger by day and late nights. Intend to come out a different person; doing better is no longer optional.

outline.heading: We were late, and children are starving
outline.gist: Because we were late, because he was late in figuring out his own life and impact, children carrying our names are starving to death. When Islam prevails it brings good to everyone, which is why we have an ethical obligation to live it and work for its success.

outline.heading: Your piece of the puzzle
outline.gist: Even if you spend your life strengthening a small community in a corner called London, Ontario, that is your piece of the puzzle: invisible from afar, but the One you do it for sees it and records it. The person no one notices may receive the greatest reward.

outline.heading: Spend the week on your why
outline.gist: They did the best they could within their limits in serving Allah, their deen and their nation. Spend the coming week asking why this Ramadan should be your turning point, find the reason that makes sense to you, and plan around it so that what is happening in Gaza never happens again.

outline.heading: Advocacy has faded: bring it back
outline.gist: He is disappointed at how the community has settled down since October and November: drag a crisis out six or seven weeks and people lose interest, though the killing and systematic starvation have not slowed. Those who were enthusiastic should bring it back as part of their Ramadan intention.

outline.heading: Outro
